summary: Children learn that a line of symmetry is a fold line: a line about which one half of a figure maps exactly onto the other. The defining idea is an operational fold-and-match test, not a counting rule. A non-square rectangle has two lines of symmetry (through the midpoints of opposite sides), not four, and its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding corner-to-corner leaves the halves misaligned (a square, the special rectangle, has 4 lines including its diagonals). Children find ALL lines in a shape, recognise shapes with none, and judge symmetry whatever the shape's orientation. The activities use physical folding of cut-out shapes and movable mirror lines to confront the common 'lines = number of sides' over-generalisation, with item-based and tappable-image formats as complementary assessment and illustration.
misconceptions: Assuming the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — so a rectangle is given 4 lines instead of 2 (over-generalised from regular shapes).
Treating a diagonal of a rectangle (or other non-square) as a line of symmetry, when folding along it shows the halves do not match.
Only recognising a line of symmetry when it is vertical/upright, missing symmetry in tilted or rotated shapes.
Thinking every shape must have at least one line of symmetry (not recognising asymmetric shapes).

activities.title: Fold-and-match test with a drawn candidate line
steps: Start with a cut-out or on-screen rectangle. Draw where you think each fold line (line of symmetry) should be, and say why before testing.
Fold (or let a screen model fold) one half across each drawn line and check whether the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Deliberately try a diagonal corner-to-corner: fold along it and watch the far corners — they miss each other, so it is NOT a line of symmetry.
Confirm the vertical and horizontal lines through the side midpoints: these fold to an exact match, so the rectangle has 2 lines, not 4.
Tilt or rotate the shape (e.g. 30-40 degrees) and re-check the same lines are still there without turning the page upright.
Progress to non-regular polygons and a few asymmetric shapes (answer: 0 lines), testing every candidate line by folding.
activities.insight: A line of symmetry is whatever survives the fold-and-match test, not whatever a count-the-sides rule predicts; symmetry is a structural property of the shape independent of its orientation.

activities.title: Movable mirror line on a geoboard or with a mirror
steps: Use a geoboard with an elastic band (or a Mira/mirror laid on a candidate line) as a movable mirror line.
Move the mirror line around the shape rather than always drawing it on an upright picture; check whether the reflection completes the shape.
Begin with symmetric patterns before moving to named shapes, recognising symmetry in patterns first.
Complete the missing half of a shape given a specific line of symmetry.
activities.insight: A mirror line can sit anywhere, and reflection across the right line reproduces the shape; recognising symmetry in patterns builds toward naming and drawing lines on shapes.

activities.title: Sort shapes by number of lines of symmetry
steps: Sort a set of shapes into 'no lines', 'exactly one line', and 'more than one line' using a Carroll or Venn arrangement.
Include non-regular and asymmetric shapes so cases with zero lines appear.
For each shape, justify its placement by the fold-and-match test rather than by counting sides.
Compare an equilateral triangle (3 lines), a square (4 lines), a rectangle (2 lines) and a regular hexagon (6 lines), and discuss when 'lines = sides' holds and when it breaks.
activities.insight: Symmetry must be tested per shape; 'lines = number of sides' holds only for regular shapes, so the equilateral triangle, square and regular hexagon match their side counts while the (non-regular) rectangle has fewer lines than its 4 sides.

activities.title: Check items and tappable-line illustration (assessment and support)
steps: Answer short items: 'How many lines of symmetry does this rectangle have?' (with 4 and 'the diagonals' as tempting wrong options), draw all lines on a given figure, decide whether a statement about a tilted shape is true or false, and sort shapes by number of lines.
Include at least one tilted shape and one asymmetric shape in any set.
As a lighter support, tap each drawn line on a static shape to reveal a fold overlay showing match or mismatch, and open a flap asking 'does the diagonal work?' answered by the mismatched fold.
activities.insight: Recognising and drawing correct lines of symmetry — especially rejecting the rectangle's diagonals and spotting tilted symmetry — demonstrates the fold-and-match concept rather than a counting habit.

checkQuestion: Show an upright rectangle (clearly not a square). Ask: 'How many lines of symmetry does this rectangle have? Draw each one. Then tell me: how do you KNOW each line you drew is a line of symmetry — and how would you decide whether a line is NOT one?'
checkAnswer: Two lines of symmetry — one vertical and one horizontal, each through the midpoints of opposite sides. The child justifies each by the fold-and-match test (folding along the line, the two halves land exactly on each other) and explains that the diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding corner-to-corner leaves the halves misaligned.
